text: From a DEFLATE stream with a missing start, ZipRec makes unique inferences for about 30% of co-indices, reconstructing about 75% of the unknown bytes with over 90% accuracy (English/Spanish text).
quote: Unique inferences can be made for approximately 30% of the co-indices, permitting reconstruction of approximately 75% of the unknown bytes recovered from the compressed data with accuracy in excess of 90%.

text: Off-the-shelf decompressors stop at the first corruption; nothing after it is recovered.
quote: However, generally-available tools do not permit recovering data after the point of corruption.

text: Block-start search statistics: fewer than 1 in 1000 bit positions yield a valid Huffman tree, 95% of those fail the end-of-block check, and over 80% of the survivors are real intact blocks, so false block starts remain possible.
quote: Fewer than 1 in 1000 possible bit positions yield valid Huffman trees; of those, 95% fail the end-of-data symbol check. Among the candidates which have a valid end-of-data symbol, over 80% are in fact valid, intact packets

text: The unknown-byte reconstruction only works for text that segments into words; scattered unknown bytes make non-textual data impractical to reconstruct.
quote: the reconstruction process described above is only suited for files which may be segmented into word-like units; in practice, this means files consisting primarily of text.

text: More reconstruction iterations raise the share of unknown bytes filled but lower the share filled correctly, because errors propagate.
quote: As expected, the percentage of reconstructed text rises with increasing iterations, while the percentage of correctly-reconstructed bytes drops due to error propagation.

text: On a Real Data Corpus disk image, 2389 of the DEFLATE streams ZipRec attempted had zero or one block, 58 had two, and 43 had more than two, so block-level resynchronization has little to work with on small streams.
quote: Among attempted decompressions, 2389 streams contained zero or one packet, 58 contained two packets, and 43 contained more than two packets.

text: Brown proposes a GUI for manual correction in which one human correction updates every co-indexed occurrence of the same unknown byte.
quote: Taking advantage of co-indexing, each time the user corrects one instance, all other co-indexed instances can be updated as well.

text: Replacing 512 bytes with random data made the DEFLATE bitstream invalid in only four of 100 runs: most corruption decodes silently.
quote: In early experiments, only four of 100 test runs replacing 512 bytes by random data generated invalid compressed bitstreams.

text: ZipRec 1.0 detects corruption automatically only when it is a run of at least 128 identical bytes (for example, zero-filled sectors).
quote: Currently, ZipRec 1.0 only detects corruption automatically where there is a sequence of at least 128 consecutive identical bytes

text: Real-world mechanism for zero runs: forensic imaging tools replace unreadable sectors with zeros (supports DMG-002 realism).
quote: file-copy utilities like dc3dd or dcfldd would generate such a sequence when they replace unreadable sectors by zeros.

text: Intra-block resynchronization: with the block's Huffman tables known, every candidate restart bit position after the corrupt region is decoded until all 48 candidates converge on the same symbol boundary.
quote: each of the 48 possible starting positions are incrementally decompressed until all of them converge on the same bit boundary

text: The candidate segmentations converge after a median of under 50 bytes, never more than 150 bytes in development testing.
quote: Convergence takes a median of less than 50 bytes and during testing in development never exceeded 150 bytes.

text: With intra-block recovery, window realignment and n-gram reconstruction, 128 to 4096 corrupted compressed bytes yield output differing from the original by less than twice the bytes the corrupted segment represented.
quote: corrupted segments of 128–4096 bytes in the compressed bit-stream result in reconstructed output which differs from the original file by an average of less than twice the number of bytes represented by the corrupted segment.

text: Evaluation damage model: a contiguous zeroed run at a fixed archive offset in Europarl plain-text ZIPs (the case its detector is built for).
quote: the specified number of bytes starting at offset 4096 within the ZIP archive were set to zero.

text: Brown scores reconstruction by recall and precision separately because wrongly reconstructed bytes, unlike bytes left unknown, can mislead the reader.
quote: Unlike unknown bytes, these may mislead the user into misreading the content of the file.

text: A replacement is accepted as high-reliability only with at least one good context and a confidence at least 0.97 times the highest score (a confidence-threshold acceptance rule).
quote: A candidate replacement is considered to be of high reliability if it has at least one good context, and its confidence score is greater than zero and at least 0.97 times the highest confidence score.

text: Automatic localisation of corruption in the general case is unsolved: two attempts failed.
quote: Two unsuccessful attempts have been made to determine corruption points automatically in the general case

text: Why they failed: language-model score drops at the corruption point are smaller than the natural variation of the scores.
quote: While both methods showed a drop in scores at the point of corruption, the natural variation in scores is larger than the drop due to corruption.

text: Inferring the Huffman tables of a block whose header is lost was infeasible in isolation; constraints from reconstructed back-references might help.
quote: This proved to be infeasible when processing the packet in isolation, but combining the search with constraints set by reconstructed back-references may lead to success.

text: Resynchronization currently discards a median of nearly 50 bytes; using reconstructed values could cut the loss to at most six bytes.
quote: limiting the loss to a maximum of six bytes instead of the current median of nearly 50.

text: Multiple corrupted regions in one file were not evaluated.
quote: While the program code supports one area of corruption in each DEFLATE packet of a file, performance with multiple areas of corruption in a single file has not yet been evaluated.

text: Highly repetitive markup (XML-style tags) is the hardest content to reconstruct; PDF content-stream operators are similarly repetitive.
quote: Experience has shown that such tags are often the most difficult to reconstruct precisely because of their highly-repetitive nature.

text: pugz accepts a candidate block start only after five more blocks decode successfully, a confirmation that single-block streams cannot provide.
quote: Once a block decompression succeeds, we decompress five more blocks to confirm that we are effectively synced to the DEFLATE stream.

text: Unknown history is represented by a window of unique symbols so every back-reference to it can be traced and resolved later.
quote: We propose here a finer technique that consists in representing the initial context using a sequence of unique symbols

text: Starting from an unknown context in real FASTQ files, only 72% (normal level) and 37% (highest level) of sequences are fully determined on average after the first sequence-resolved block.
quote: However at the normal and highest compression levels, only respectively 72% and 37% of sequences on average are fully determined after a sequence-resolved block.

text: Block-boundary detection is tuned for ASCII; binary data needs more careful boundary determination.
quote: Furthermore, it may be possible to decompress non-ASCII (binary) files, but this would require more careful determination of block boundaries.

text: Guessing the undetermined characters left by the unknown context was not explored.
quote: It did not escape our attention that guessing those undetermined characters could be possible, but we did not yet explore this direction.

text: E-APR analyses 2,141 bugs from 130 projects and 23,551 repair attempts by Java repair tools.
quote: In total, we consider 2,141 bugs from 130 projects, and 23,551 repair attempts.

text: Repair-technique effectiveness depends on instance features; no technique is best in all cases.
quote: the effectiveness of APRTs is impacted by software features, which makes these methods problem dependent, and as such, no technique can be considered the best in all cases.

text: A random-forest selector predicts the most suitable repair technique per bug with 88% precision, 81% recall and 84% F1.
quote: The Random Forest Classifier is the best performing Machine Learning technique for APRT selection, and can predict the most suitable technique with 88% precision, 81% recall and 84% f1-score.

text: The selector is trained on plausible repairs (tests pass), not correct ones.
quote: In our experiment from Section 4 we consider all generated patches (plausible) rather than focusing only on correct patches.

text: Correctness-labelled data were too scarce: only 20 correctly repaired bugs, not enough to learn footprints.
quote: We found that the dataset consisting of 20 bugs that were correctly repaired is not sufficient for the machine learning algorithms used to identify significant features and create the algorithm footprints.

text: Existing repair infrastructures run a fixed tool order or leave the choice to the user (RepairThemAll has 11 tools and no selection guidance).
quote: RepairThemAll has 11 automated repair techniques, but it does not offer any capabilities or guidelines in terms of which technique to select.

text: The IETF replaced SCTP's Adler-32 because it detects errors weakly on small inputs.
quote: For small packets Adler-32 provides weak detection of errors.

text: For short inputs Adler-32's first sum cannot wrap (128 bytes sum to at most 32640), so checksum values cluster.
quote: There are only 128 bytes of input, so the greatest value which the s1 accumulator can have is 255 * 128 = 32640.

text: Clustered checksum values make it likelier that a damaged input still passes the check.
quote: the likelihood of even a 'small' error leaving a damaged packet with a valid checksum is higher than if all checksum values are equally likely

text: Salvage after a lost start: try decompression at every bit offset until a few DEFLATE blocks decode, priming a faux dictionary to avoid distance-too-far errors.
quote: You will need to attempt decompression starting at every bit until you get successful decoding for at least a few deflate blocks.

text: Reliability test: decode a second time with a different dummy dictionary; only output identical in both runs is independent of the lost history.
quote: decompress again with a different dictionary to detect unreliable data

text: Dependence on the missing history can persist far into the stream (any repeated string from the lost part keeps propagating).
quote: The next half is to find where in the deflate stream there is no longer a dependence on the unknown uncompressed data derived from that missing 361 bytes of compressed data.

text: Real flash damage: the estimated bitflip rate is about one bitflip every 248253 bytes (supports DMG-007 realism).
quote: This yields a p equal to 5.03 ˆ 10´7 or equivalently, one bitflip every 248253 bytes.
